Motor boat enthusiasts and all those who go in for aquatic pressures during the coming season are given valuable advice by Leslie Huxtable, principal of the Motor Boat School of the west Side Young Men's Christian Association, New York.

"Look to the life ring" warns Mr. Huxtable. "Every owner of a boat of any kind should practise throwing with the life ring. First get a good life ring and then not less than a hundred feet of room rope to attach to the ring. The life ring is an awkward thing to handle and it requires practice to drop it in the right place, for the sake of the guests the motor coat owner should know how to throw a ring accurately, for no one knows when a friend may fall into the water and be carried away by the tire. On such occasions every second counts. So have your ring heavy, have the rope properly arranged so that it will not foul and then know how to throw it. A few hours practice will make most men proficient. Then keep in practice by throwing the ring every few days".

For the purpose of illustrating the right way to handle the life ring Mr. Huxtable consented to accompany a photographer to the float of the society, where the accompany inc pictures were snapped. They show:
No. 1. How to keep the life ring handy and ready for instant use.
No. 2. Correct way to hold life ring, one foot on ball, rope on arm so it feeds off easily.

A mountain in climbing elmoxhakesenx club has been organized in Philadelphia. All the outfit needed is about sixty feet of half inch manila rope. The "mountains" can be found within walking distance of almost any town. Any steep rocky hillside that cannot be scaled under ordinary conditions will do. On a recent trip the mountain climbers of Philadelphia selected an almost perpendicular declivity near Swarthmore. A few narrow ledges afforded precarious foothold, but for the most part the climb was as straight and steep as the side of a house. The rope afforded the only means of getting to the top.

A member of the club who had had some mountain climbing experience abroad showed how it was possible to lasso a rock that justed out near the top and provided a safe anchorage for the rope, and with this as a help it was found possible to scale the steep. Some skill, a lot of nerve and considerable athletic ability were necessary to reach the top and this combination of qualities gave rest to the task and provided the thrills necessary to make the mountain climbing experience one to be remembered. Every one knows the keen delight of overcoming obstacles. The feat of climbing to the top off an apparently inaccessible hill affords an opportunity for enjoying to the full this pleasurable experience. Besides which it is one of the finest exercises imaginable to climb hand over hand up above a rope stretched from the top of a steep straight cliff, with the toes digging in the bare stone for a support and the knowledge that there is no turning back, but that the top must be reached at any cost.

It is given to few to go to Europe and attempt to climb the mountains here, but any one can idulge indulge the fancy at home and doubtless find as much enjoyment as in seeking to out do the daring climbers who risk their lives in the peaks of the continental mountain region.

How crooked butchers, bakers, grocers and delica*essen men have waxed rich on unsuspecting New York purchasers is eloquently shown to-day by Commissioner of Weights and Measures Joseph Hartigan. In the park between City Hall and the County Court House is displayed as villainous a collection of fake pint, quart, gallon and bushel measures and scales as was ever brought together in this city.

The widow who bought the quart of milk that seemed so small didn't know that the pudgy, honest-eyed corner grocer sold it from a dipper that had a false bottom. These dips are shown in to-day's rogues' gallery of tinware. All were seized in this city. From the locations of the seizures, both Riverside Drive and Rington Street suffered equally from this form of daylight robbery.

And then there are potato baskets, peach baskets, oil cans and ice scales that are works of black art. Inside the regular sized peach basket of several quarts capacity is woven another of just half the size. This means that for every quart the dishonest wholesaler or retailer sells he steals the price of another.

There is a "five-gallon" oil can on exhibit. Inside is another can of just two and a half gallons. When you try to fill the big can you succeed in filling only the inside can. This is where the dishonest oil dealer puts one over on Mr. Corner Grocer. It is a sort of retribution for the widow
who was cheated out of her just share of milk.
The most daring illustration of crookedness of dishonest measures is that of a "five-gallon" milk can. Fitted into the neck of the measure is a quart can.

If a grocer is busy and the whole-saler is delivering from a wagon, he can sell a quart of milk and get paid for five gallons. But this plan was too good to last and the owner of the can is serving time.

If the get-rich-quick ice dealer needs the price of a new automobile all he has to do is shift the fulcrum of the scale just about half an inch. It requires the eye of an eagle to see it, but it nets a fortune on a hot day when the world is yelling for ice.

That's where the crooked grocer, butcher and delicatessen man heats your pocketbook and stomach alike.
Even the penny weighing machines are not all on the level. One fat woman told Commissioner Hartigan they are "gay deceivers."

"Only skinny people weigh themselves often," said the stout lady. "They are worried and think they are going into a decline. The ceremony consisted of a surprise visit paid to a house by a party of neighbors. Just before dawn the visiting party drew their canoes together and covered them with planks, thereby making a floor on which they performed a wild dance to the sound of shouting, intended to arouse the inmates of the visited house. In this picture, the dancers are seen in the background, and the surprised host is in the foreground, summoning his household to welcome the visitors and join in the celebration. The aim of the visitors is to take the visited brave entirely by surprise; his aim is to forestall them in dispensing hospitality. If he failed to do this, he was much chagrined. The friendly rivalry on this point was very keen.

The House-Buildors (Haida) -

The building is one of those elaborate houses which were the height of a Haida Indian's ambition. Wooling Ceremony (Nootka) -

When a Hootka brave sought a bride, he asked a dozen of his friends to assist him to transport gifts to the girls father. It was customary for the father of dutiful and nimiable daughters to return such gifts to the bride-groom. In such cases the bride had the tribal right to leave her husband if she became dissatisfied. If her father, however, had kept the gifts, signifying that she had not been up to the traditional standard of nimiability and dutifulness, the bride's position as a wife was little better than that of a slave. Potlatch Ceremony (Kwakriutl) -

In gifts made periodically, each chief tried to outdo his neighbor in generosity. In this way the chiefs showed their hospitality and exhibited their own wealth and ability to acquire wealth. Here the young chief stands upon an elevation before his house, entertaining the followers of a neighboring chief who had previously made him gifts, while his own followers bring sufficient gifts to eclipse the neighbor's generosity of some months earlier. These gifts were made at intervals of six months or a year, and were always made between the same two groups of Indians. Each chief and his followers, when their turn came to make the gift, made every effort to make the greatest display possible, and gave all they had and frequently went into debt in order to achieve their purpose.

It takes an entire year to make one of these great Robes,的比例 of it and finish it off in style. The price paid is little enough compensation for the twix toil involved.

"I am already at work on the robe ordered by one of the masquersaders next year. This man gives me some sort of an idea of what he wants and leaves me to work it out. Everything is done by hand and you can see by the size of the robe what an enormous amount of work it is to complete a robe with its vast quantity of embryodery in various colors.

"I have lately adopted a new rule. I don't sell the robot outright, but permit it to be used on the occasion for which it is ordered and then when I get it back I hire it out again to some one of the masqueraders in some other city. It is impossible to wear the same robot twice in the same city, no matter how long a time may elapse between the times of wearing, for the reason that women at least will remember every line of the robot that passed before them stretched from curb to curb and they would know the garter again in a moment. "There is enough material in one of these big Robes to make a score of small suits for masqueraders and when I have covered the country with this one I shall then cut it up and use it for a number of suits.
